distractorExplanations.a: That is roughly where the low-air warning must activate, far below the governor cut-out point.
distractorExplanations.b: This is below even the cut-in point; the compressor would never stop pumping at a normal level.
distractorExplanations.c: About 100 psi is the governor cut-in point, where the compressor resumes pumping, not cut-out.

distractorExplanations.a: Around 60 psi is the low-air warning point; cut-in happens well above it, near 100 psi.
distractorExplanations.c: Too high; per the CDL manual the compressor resumes pumping at about 100 psi.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the governor cut-out range where the compressor stops pumping, not where it resumes.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-systems-0.explanation: Cut-in is typically ~100 psi so the compressor resumes charging. Use the manufacturer specification if it differs.

options.a: Receives compressed air first and helps remove moisture/oil
options.b: Stores air for the secondary circuit that feeds the front axle
options.c: Supplies air directly to the trailer through the red gladhand
options.d: Collects air last, after the primary and secondary tanks fill

distractorExplanations.b: That is the secondary (dry) reservoir; the supply tank receives air first and collects moisture and oil.
distractorExplanations.c: Trailer supply air passes through the tractor protection valve from the service reservoirs, not straight from the wet tank.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the order: the supply (wet) tank is the first reservoir after the compressor and dryer.

options.a: Two compressors, one for the tractor and one for the trailer
options.b: Separate service and parking brake systems on the same axle
options.c: Two independent service air circuits (primary/secondary)
options.d: Air-over-hydraulic brakes, with air boosting a hydraulic system

distractorExplanations.a: A dual system has one compressor feeding two separate service circuits; the trailer is supplied by the tractor.
distractorExplanations.b: Every air-brake vehicle has service and spring (parking) brakes; dual refers to two service circuits.
distractorExplanations.d: Air-over-hydraulic is a different brake type; a dual air system has primary and secondary air circuits.

options.a: A separate electric motor
options.b: The transmission output shaft
options.c: The engine (gear/belt/drive)
options.d: The power steering pump shaft

distractorExplanations.a: Truck air compressors are driven by the engine through gears or a belt, not a separate electric motor.
distractorExplanations.b: The compressor turns whenever the engine runs, even when parked, so it is not driven off the driveline.
distractorExplanations.d: The power steering pump is a separate accessory; the compressor is driven directly by the engine.

options.a: Cool compressed air so the governor can cut out sooner
options.b: Store reserve air for the parking brake if tanks leak down
options.c: Remove moisture (and much oil/contaminants) before tanks
options.d: Release built-up pressure if the governor fails to cut out

distractorExplanations.a: Cut-out timing is set by the governor; the dryer's job is removing moisture and oil from the air.
distractorExplanations.b: The dryer stores no reserve air; spring brakes apply mechanically when air pressure is lost.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the safety relief valve's job (opens around 150 psi), not the air dryer's.

options.a: 20 psi
options.b: 30 psi
options.c: 45 psi
options.d: 60 psi

distractorExplanations.a: About 20 psi is near the bottom of the spring-brake application range; the warning comes much earlier.
distractorExplanations.b: At 30 psi the spring brakes may already be applying; the warning must sound before pressure falls below 60.
distractorExplanations.c: 45 psi is the upper end of the spring-brake application range, too late for the low-air warning.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-systems-0.explanation: FMVSS/CDL texts: warn by ~60 psi. Some manufacturers set it slightly lower (about 55–60 psi).

options.a: Spring force into air pressure for the parking brakes
options.b: Air pressure into mechanical force at the slack/pushrod
options.c: Pedal force into air pressure for the brake lines
options.d: Mechanical force into air pressure for the reservoirs

distractorExplanations.a: Reversed: spring brakes apply mechanically when air is released; chambers turn air into force.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the foot (treadle) valve, which meters reservoir air when the pedal is pressed.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes the compressor; brake chambers turn air pressure into pushrod force.

options.a: Faster build-up time because the governor stays cut in
options.b: Higher tank pressure as the safety valve compensates
options.c: Spring brakes releasing once pressure drops below 60 psi
options.d: Longer build-up time and possible spring-brake application

distractorExplanations.a: A leak wastes compressed air, so build-up takes longer, not shorter.
distractorExplanations.b: The safety valve only vents overpressure; a leak lowers pressure and lengthens build-up time.
distractorExplanations.c: Spring brakes apply, not release, as pressure falls (typically about 20–45 psi).

options.a: Increase front braking force on slippery surfaces to aid steering
options.b: Can reduce front application on slippery surfaces
options.c: Limit trailer brake pressure so the trailer does not push the tractor
options.d: Hold front brakes released until rear brakes have fully applied

distractorExplanations.a: Opposite effect: the limiting valve cuts front brake pressure on slick roads to reduce front lockup.
distractorExplanations.c: These valves act on the tractor's front (steer) axle, not on trailer brake pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: They reduce front application pressure; they do not delay front brakes until the rear applies.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-systems-0.explanation: Some systems proportion front braking; modern ABS changes practice. The exact behavior is design-dependent, and modern ABS has changed practice.

options.a: Applies tractor spring brakes when trailer air pressure drops
options.b: Protects tractor air if trailer breaks away / supply is lost
options.c: Prevents service and spring brake forces from compounding
options.d: Releases the trailer brakes after a breakaway so it can be towed

distractorExplanations.a: The TP valve closes to keep tractor air; tractor springs apply only if tractor air itself is lost.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the anti-compounding valve's job, not the tractor protection valve's.
distractorExplanations.d: After a breakaway the trailer emergency brakes apply; the TP valve protects tractor air instead.

options.a: Helps prevent wheel lockup during hard braking
options.b: Shortens stopping distance on every road surface
options.c: Lets the driver keep pumping brakes during a stop
options.d: Takes over braking if the service brakes fail

distractorExplanations.b: ABS keeps steering control; it may not shorten stops and can lengthen them on loose gravel or snow.
distractorExplanations.c: With ABS the driver applies steady firm pressure; pumping interferes with ABS modulation.
distractorExplanations.d: ABS only modulates normal service brakes; it adds no braking power if the brakes fail.

options.a: Store emergency air for applying the spring brakes
options.b: Connect the chamber pushrod to the S-cam/foundation brake
options.c: Meter air from the foot valve to each brake chamber
options.d: Control air pressure in the tanks between cut-in and cut-out

distractorExplanations.a: Slack adjusters store no air; spring brakes apply mechanically when chamber air is released.
distractorExplanations.c: Metering air is done by the foot valve and relay valves; slack adjusters link pushrod to S-cam.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the governor's role; slack adjusters are mechanical levers at each wheel end.

options.a: Reduced braking capability; stop safely and treat as emergency
options.b: Full braking, since the other circuit doubles its pressure
options.c: Spring brakes applying at once on all axles to stop the truck
options.d: Normal braking until the next scheduled stop or inspection

distractorExplanations.b: The remaining circuit does not compensate; losing one circuit reduces total braking capability.
distractorExplanations.c: Springs apply only when pressure falls low; losing one circuit leaves the other circuit's service brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Braking is reduced immediately; the CDL manual says stop safely and get the system repaired.

options.a: 2 psi/min single or 3 psi/min combination
options.b: 3 psi/min single or 4 psi/min combination
options.c: 4 psi/min single or 5 psi/min combination
options.d: 5 psi/min single or 6 psi/min combination

distractorExplanations.a: Those are the released-brake leakage limits; with brakes applied the limits are 3 and 4 psi/min.
distractorExplanations.c: Too lenient by 1 psi/min; the applied-brake limit is 3 psi/min single and 4 psi/min combination.
distractorExplanations.d: Far above the handbook limits; that much loss with brakes applied means the vehicle needs repair.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-inspectio.explanation: Applied leakage limits are slightly higher than released. These are the CDL handbook figures.

options.a: Governor cut-in pressure, about 100 psi
options.b: The low-air warning point, about 60 psi
options.c: Just above spring-brake pop-out, about 45 psi
options.d: Governor cut-out / normal operating pressure

distractorExplanations.a: The leakage test starts from a fully charged system at cut-out, not from the cut-in point.
distractorExplanations.b: Starting at 60 psi could trigger the warning and springs; the test begins at full operating pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the spring-brake application range; leakage is checked from full charge at governor cut-out.

options.a: ~20–45 psi range depending on system
options.b: ~55–60 psi, as the low-air warning sounds
options.c: ~90–100 psi, near governor cut-in pressure
options.d: ~120–125 psi, near governor cut-out pressure

distractorExplanations.b: The low-air warning comes first at about 60 psi; springs apply later, as pressure falls to about 20–45.
distractorExplanations.c: Around 100 psi is governor cut-in; springs stay released until pressure drops far lower.
distractorExplanations.d: 125 psi is normal full charge at cut-out; spring brakes apply only after major air loss.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-inspectio.explanation: As service air falls, springs take over. Know your own vehicle's figure.

options.a: Brake linings are new and still bedding in; recheck later
options.b: The slack adjuster is set too tight; back it off a turn
options.c: Air pressure is too high; lower the governor cut-out setting
options.d: Brakes may be weak/unsafe; adjust or repair per procedure

distractorExplanations.a: Excessive pushrod stroke is an adjustment or mechanical defect, not a lining break-in condition.
distractorExplanations.b: Out-of-adjustment brakes usually overstroke because they are too loose; backing off makes it worse.
distractorExplanations.c: Stroke is measured at a set application pressure; changing governor settings does not fix adjustment.

options.a: Gladhands only, since lines are sealed
options.b: Tank drain valves and the governor alone
options.c: Hoses, fittings, chambers, valves, tanks
options.d: The dash gauges, buzzer, and warning light

distractorExplanations.a: Leaks occur anywhere in the system: hoses, fittings, chambers, valves and tanks, not just gladhands.
distractorExplanations.b: Drain valves and the governor are only two of many leak points; hoses, fittings and chambers also leak.
distractorExplanations.d: Gauges and warnings show pressure loss; the leak survey checks physical air components.

options.a: Within about 10 seconds under test conditions
options.b: Within about 20 seconds under test conditions
options.c: Within about 30 seconds under test conditions
options.d: Within about 45 seconds under test conditions

distractorExplanations.a: The handbook standard for dual systems is 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds; 10 seconds is not the benchmark.
distractorExplanations.b: 20 seconds is not the CDL handbook benchmark; dual systems should build 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: The handbook build-up standard is 45 seconds for 85 to 100 psi; 30 seconds understates the allowed time.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-inspectio.explanation: Slow build-up suggests compressor/drive/leak issues. Use the OEM figure if it differs from the handbook.

options.a: Weekly, once the air dryer purge stops
options.b: Monthly, during scheduled PM service
options.c: Daily/as required to remove water and oil
options.d: Only when the air dryer is not working

distractorExplanations.a: Water and oil collect daily; tanks without automatic drains are drained at least daily or as required.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting a month lets water and oil build up, causing freezing and valve failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Even with a working dryer, tanks still need daily/as-required draining to remove moisture and oil.

options.a: Indicate a foundation brake problem needing repair, not endless readjustment
options.b: Are working normally, since automatic adjusters need manual tweaks every week
options.c: Should be backed off so pushrod stroke stays at its maximum limit
options.d: Should be replaced by manual slack adjusters on that axle for good

distractorExplanations.b: Automatic slack adjusters should not need routine manual adjustment; repeated overstroke signals a defect.
distractorExplanations.c: Running at maximum stroke leaves no reserve and risks out-of-service brakes; the root cause needs repair.
distractorExplanations.d: Automatic slack adjusters have been required on new air-braked vehicles since 1994; repair, do not downgrade.

options.a: Drive to the next terminal if ABS still works
options.b: Acceptable if braking feels normal on a test stop
options.c: Remove from service / repair before dispatch
options.d: Cool it with water, then recheck before driving

distractorExplanations.a: ABS cannot compensate for a cracked friction surface; the drum or rotor must be repaired first.
distractorExplanations.b: A normal-feeling stop does not prove a cracked drum is safe; cracks can fail suddenly under heat and load.
distractorExplanations.d: Water on a hot drum can widen cracks; a cracked drum or rotor is a repair item, not a cooling issue.

options.a: Normal lubrication carried over from the brake chamber diaphragms
options.b: Engine coolant leaking into the governor line
options.c: Compressor passing oil / dryer issues / maintenance needed
options.d: Spring-brake grease migrating back up the lines into the tank

distractorExplanations.a: Chamber diaphragms are rubber and produce no oil; oil in the tank comes from the compressor.
distractorExplanations.b: Coolant would show as a sweet-smelling, colored fluid; oil carryover points to the compressor or dryer.
distractorExplanations.d: Grease in brake components cannot travel upstream into reservoirs; oil comes from compressor carryover.

options.a: Coupled with seals removed for a tighter metal fit
options.b: Hooked to dummy couplers while pulling a trailer
options.c: Clean, sealed, correctly coupled, undamaged
options.d: Crossed service-to-supply if the colors are faded

distractorExplanations.a: Gladhands seal through rubber grommets; removing seals causes leaks rather than a tighter fit.
distractorExplanations.b: Dummy couplers are for bobtailing; with a trailer the gladhands must be coupled to the trailer.
distractorExplanations.d: Supply goes to supply and service to service; crossed lines can leave the trailer without brakes.

options.a: Lamp should stay off at start-up, since lighting at all means a fault
options.b: Lamp should flash until the air pressure reaches governor cut-out
options.c: Lamp should illuminate then go out if system passes self-check
options.d: Lamp should stay on whenever the parking brake is set

distractorExplanations.a: The lamp lighting briefly at start-up is the normal bulb check; staying on is what signals a fault.
distractorExplanations.b: The ABS lamp is not tied to air pressure; it does a bulb check and goes out if ABS passes self-test.
distractorExplanations.d: The ABS lamp reports ABS faults, not parking brake status, which has its own indicator.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-inspectio.explanation: Bulb/self-check is part of pre-trip. Timing of the lamp check is vehicle-specific.

options.a: Drain the tanks and keep driving if pressure stays above 60
options.b: Raise the governor cut-out setting to compensate for leaks
options.c: Check belts/drive, leaks, governor, dryer, filter restrictions
options.d: Pump the brake pedal to help the compressor build pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Slow build-up signals a charging fault that needs diagnosis; draining tanks does not fix it.
distractorExplanations.b: Raising cut-out does not speed charging and can overpressure the system; find the cause first.
distractorExplanations.d: Pumping the pedal uses air and slows build-up; the compressor charges the tanks on its own.

options.a: Apply lightly and steadily without lockup
options.b: Pump rapidly on and off before wheels lock
options.c: Apply fully, release as wheels lock, reapply
options.d: Apply fully and hold until the vehicle stops

distractorExplanations.a: That is controlled braking; stab braking means full application, release on lockup, reapply.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid pumping wastes air and is not the stab method; the brakes are applied fully until wheels lock.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding locked wheels removes steering control; stab braking releases when the wheels lock.

options.a: Pump the pedal so ABS can reset between pulses
options.b: Use stab braking: apply, release, and reapply
options.c: Apply the trailer hand valve before the pedal
options.d: Apply firm steady pressure and let ABS modulate

distractorExplanations.a: Pumping interrupts ABS; it already pulses the brakes, so the driver holds steady firm pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Stab braking is for vehicles without ABS; with ABS, apply firm steady pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: The hand valve can cause trailer skids and is not used for stopping; use the service pedal with ABS.

options.a: Increased brake grab
options.b: Higher air pressure use
options.c: Reduced braking power
options.d: Tighter brake adjustment

distractorExplanations.a: Heat makes linings less effective and drums expand away from them, so braking weakens, not grabs.
distractorExplanations.b: Fade is a friction loss from heat, not a change in air pressure consumption.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot drums expand, effectively loosening adjustment and lengthening stroke, which reduces braking.

options.a: Start in a higher gear and downshift as the speed builds on the grade
options.b: Select a safe speed/gear early; use braking without overheating
options.c: Hold light, steady brake pressure the whole way down
options.d: Use the trailer hand valve to hold the speed down on the grade

distractorExplanations.a: Downshifting on a downgrade may be impossible once speed builds; select the low gear before the grade.
distractorExplanations.c: Constant light braking overheats the brakes and causes fade; use the right gear and snub braking.
distractorExplanations.d: Using the hand valve to brake can overheat trailer brakes and cause skids; use gear and service brakes.

options.a: Hold light, steady pressure to keep speed constant
options.b: Apply firmly to reduce speed, release to cool, repeat
options.c: Pump the brakes rapidly to keep the linings cool
options.d: Apply the trailer brakes only and let the tractor coast

distractorExplanations.a: Continuous light pressure builds heat and causes fade; snub braking applies firmly and then releases.
distractorExplanations.c: Rapid pumping wastes air and does not cool brakes; snub braking uses firm applications with release intervals.
distractorExplanations.d: Braking with only the trailer overheats its brakes and risks a skid; snub braking uses the service brakes.

options.a: Hold the lockup and steer gently toward the shoulder
options.b: Release to regain steering, then reapply as needed
options.c: Pump the trailer hand valve until the wheels unlock
options.d: Set the parking brake to stop in the shortest distance

distractorExplanations.a: Locked front wheels cannot steer; release the brakes to regain steering before reapplying.
distractorExplanations.c: The hand valve controls only trailer brakes and can cause a trailer skid; release the pedal instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Spring brakes give no lockup control and can cause a skid; release and reapply the service brakes.

options.a: Fade until the engine retarder dries the drums
options.b: Lock up until air pressure is rebuilt to cut-out
options.c: Pull or grab until dried by light application
options.d: Work normally once the ABS lamp goes out

distractorExplanations.a: Wet brakes are weak or uneven because of water, and the retarder does not dry them; light braking does.
distractorExplanations.b: Water affects friction, not air pressure; brakes may pull or grab until dried by light application.
distractorExplanations.d: The ABS lamp does not indicate wet brakes; dry them with light application while driving slowly.

options.a: Set the trailer hand valve and leave the transmission in gear
options.b: Apply the service brakes with the hand valve and turn off the engine
options.c: Apply parking brake; consider wheel chocks/curb technique as trained
options.d: Rely on the transmission in low gear, with chocks used only on ice

distractorExplanations.a: The hand valve uses service air that can leak away; it is never a parking brake.
distractorExplanations.b: Service brakes held by air will release as pressure leaks; use the spring parking brake and chocks.
distractorExplanations.d: The transmission is not a parking brake; set the parking brake and chock as trained on any grade.

options.a: Holding the trailer parked during short stops
options.b: Releasing the trailer spring brakes
options.c: Applying trailer brakes independently
options.d: Supplying air to charge the trailer tanks

distractorExplanations.a: The hand valve uses service air that can leak off; it must not be used as a parking brake.
distractorExplanations.b: Trailer spring brakes are released with the red trailer air supply valve, not the hand valve.
distractorExplanations.d: Charging trailer tanks is done by the trailer air supply (red) valve; the hand valve applies trailer brakes.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-operation.explanation: Limited trailer control; not a parking brake. It is for testing and control, not for parking.

options.a: Pump the brakes to rebuild air pressure
options.b: Continue to a shop if pressure stays above 40
options.c: Push in the red knob to restore trailer air
options.d: Safe stop ASAP; do not continue normally

distractorExplanations.a: Pumping uses more air and speeds up spring-brake application; stop safely as soon as possible.
distractorExplanations.b: At 40 psi the springs may be close to applying; low air means stop safely right away.
distractorExplanations.c: Pushing the red knob sends more tractor air to the trailer; it does not fix the loss of pressure.

options.a: Pulling, wheel lock, or trailer swing
options.b: Faster build-up time after each stop
options.c: Low-air warning at normal pressure
options.d: Spring brakes failing to release

distractorExplanations.b: Brake imbalance is about uneven braking force at wheel ends, not air build-up time.
distractorExplanations.c: The low-air warning reflects reservoir pressure, not uneven force between foundation brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Spring brake release depends on supply air and the chambers, not on foundation brake balance.

options.a: Release the tractor parking brakes while still coupled
options.b: Cut out the compressor and stop air buildup
options.c: Dump trailer air / apply trailer springs unexpectedly
options.d: Apply the tractor service brakes along with the trailer

distractorExplanations.a: Tractor parking brakes use the yellow valve; the red valve controls trailer air supply.
distractorExplanations.b: The governor controls compressor cut-out; the red valve does not affect air buildup.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling the red valve affects the trailer supply and trailer springs, not the tractor service brakes.

options.a: Service + spring brake force stacking that can damage components
options.b: Trailer air loss draining the tractor's own air supply after a breakaway
options.c: Overpressure in the tanks when the governor fails to cut the compressor out
options.d: Wheel lockup on slippery roads during a hard stop

distractorExplanations.b: Isolating tractor air from a trailer leak is the tractor protection valve's job.
distractorExplanations.c: Overpressure is handled by the safety relief valve, which opens around 150 psi.
distractorExplanations.d: Preventing lockup is the ABS function; anti-compounding prevents stacked service and spring force.

options.a: As long as the brakes hold on a tug test
options.b: Set by feel, with 2 inches of free play at the pedal
options.c: Within manufacturer/FMVSS limits at applied pressure
options.d: Within limits when checked with air released only

distractorExplanations.a: A tug test checks coupling or parking brake holding, not whether pushrod stroke is within limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Stroke is measured at the chamber pushrod against chamber-size limits, not by pedal free play.
distractorExplanations.d: Applied stroke is measured with about 90–100 psi applied; released position alone shows nothing.

options.a: Replace service brakes in emergency stops
options.b: Help control speed and reduce service-brake heat
options.c: Prevent wheel lockup on slippery road surfaces
options.d: Hold the vehicle stationary when parked on grades

distractorExplanations.a: Retarders are supplemental; they cannot stop the vehicle and are not used in place of service brakes.
distractorExplanations.c: Retarders can actually cause drive-wheel skids on slippery roads; ABS prevents lockup.
distractorExplanations.d: Retarders only work when the driveline is turning; they cannot hold a parked vehicle.

options.a: Apply spring brakes; vehicle will stop hard—steer to safe area if possible
options.b: Leave the vehicle without brakes until the driver sets the parking valve
options.c: Trigger the tractor protection valve, keeping tractor brakes normal
options.d: Release the spring brakes so the vehicle coasts to a gradual stop

distractorExplanations.b: Spring brakes apply by themselves as air drops; they do not wait for the driver to set them.
distractorExplanations.c: The TP valve protects tractor air from trailer leaks; with total air loss the springs apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Spring brakes are held off by air, so losing air applies them rather than releasing them.

options.a: Release the trailer brakes to avoid a skid
options.b: Apply the tractor spring brakes immediately
options.c: Protect tractor air supply from total loss
options.d: Raise governor cut-out to make up the loss

distractorExplanations.a: In a breakaway the trailer's emergency brakes apply; the TP valve closes to protect tractor air.
distractorExplanations.b: The TP valve keeps tractor air; tractor springs apply only if the tractor's own air is lost.
distractorExplanations.d: The governor setting does not change in a breakaway; the TP valve seals off the open lines.

options.a: Spring brakes applying on all axles at once
options.b: Faster stops due to air sent to other wheels
options.c: Pulling/reduced braking on that wheel end
options.d: Normal braking until the tanks drop to 60 psi

distractorExplanations.a: A ruptured service line affects that one chamber; springs apply only after major reservoir loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Air escaping from one line reduces force at that wheel; it does not boost the others.
distractorExplanations.d: Braking at that wheel is lost immediately when the line ruptures, before any tank warning.

options.a: Faster governor cut-out and higher tank pressure
options.b: Overheated drums from excess lining friction
options.c: Valve freezing, sticking, leaks, poor braking
options.d: ABS lamp staying lit with no effect on braking

distractorExplanations.a: Contamination clogs and freezes valves; it does not change governor settings or raise tank pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Drum overheating comes from braking practice; air contamination affects valves, seals and lines.
distractorExplanations.d: Water and oil can freeze or stick valves and weaken braking; they are not just a warning-lamp issue.

options.a: Grab; pump brakes to cool them
options.b: Lock; spray water on drums
options.c: Fade; keep braking harder
options.d: Fade; stop to cool when safe

distractorExplanations.a: Overheated brakes lose friction (fade); pumping keeps adding heat and wastes air.
distractorExplanations.b: Hot brakes fade rather than lock, and water on hot drums can crack them.
distractorExplanations.c: Braking harder on faded brakes adds heat and worsens fade; stop safely and let them cool.

options.a: Normal braking is lost; stop at once and wait for a tow
options.b: Spring brakes will apply soon; pull over before they lock
options.c: System may not prevent lockup; drive more carefully and get service
options.d: Traction control is off, but ABS still works at highway speed

distractorExplanations.a: ABS failure leaves normal service braking; you lose anti-lock function, not the brakes.
distractorExplanations.b: The ABS lamp is unrelated to air pressure or spring brakes; it reports an ABS fault.
distractorExplanations.d: A lit ABS lamp means anti-lock may not function at any speed; get it serviced soon.

options.a: ABS warning lamp lighting and modulators shutting off
options.b: Spring brakes releasing because supply pressure spikes
options.c: Air dryer heater failure and frozen purge valve
options.d: Overpressure / pop-off valve discharge / possible damage

distractorExplanations.a: The governor controls compressor loading; its failure does not shut down ABS modulators.
distractorExplanations.b: Spring brakes are already released at normal pressure; governor faults do not change that.
distractorExplanations.c: The dryer heater is electrical and separate; a governor fault affects pressure regulation.

options.a: ABS lamp lighting with modulators shut off
options.b: Tractor protection valve closing at speed
options.c: Brake fade from overheated drums
options.d: Low air pressure / warning / spring risk

distractorExplanations.a: A governor fault affects compressor loading and tank pressure, not the ABS electronics.
distractorExplanations.b: The TP valve closes on trailer air loss; it is not triggered by a governor fault.
distractorExplanations.c: Fade comes from heat during braking, not from a governor failure.

options.a: Raising governor cut-out to push ice out
options.b: Running the tanks at low pressure overnight
options.c: Warming valves with an open flame torch
options.d: Proper dryer maintenance and tank draining

distractorExplanations.a: Higher pressure does not clear ice and risks overpressure; keeping air dry prevents freezing.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressure level does not stop moisture freezing; dryer maintenance and draining remove the water.
distractorExplanations.c: Open flame can damage valves and hoses and is a fire hazard; prevent ice by keeping the air dry.

options.a: Build pressure to cut-out, then drive slowly so friction frees them
options.b: Cage the spring brakes on the roadside without training
options.c: Check air supply, parking control, valves, freezing, mechanical bind
options.d: Pump the service brake pedal repeatedly until the springs release

distractorExplanations.a: Driving against applied brakes overheats and damages them; find the cause first.
distractorExplanations.b: Caging without training is dangerous and leaves the axle without parking brakes; diagnose first.
distractorExplanations.d: Pumping uses air and cannot release spring brakes, which need supply air pressure.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-failures-.explanation: Diagnose safely. Do not force-drive against brakes that will not release.

options.a: Normal feel once pressure passes 100
options.b: Low pressure, leaks, or slow build-up
options.c: Air in the hydraulic master cylinder
options.d: Brakes adjusted too tight at the slack

distractorExplanations.a: A soft feel is not normal at any pressure; it suggests low air, leaks or slow build-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Pure air-brake systems have no hydraulic master cylinder; that applies to hydraulic brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Overly tight brakes drag; a soft, weak feel points to low pressure or long stroke.

options.a: ABS on the tractor, which adds wheel slip on dry roads
options.b: Lower speed, which reduces engine braking
options.c: Speed, weight, poor brakes, and downhill grades
options.d: Cold drums, which lose friction until they warm up

distractorExplanations.a: ABS reduces lockup and does not add slip; stopping distance grows with speed, weight and bad brakes.
distractorExplanations.b: Lower speed shortens stopping distance; higher speed is what increases it.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot drums lose friction (fade); cold drums do not lengthen emergency stops.

options.a: Trust the gauge, since the warning buzzer is set too high on most trucks
options.b: Trust the buzzer and continue if the gauge reads above 60 psi
options.c: Believe the more conservative indication and stop safely; get inspected
options.d: Recalibrate the gauge at the next stop and keep driving normally

distractorExplanations.a: When indicators disagree, treat the worse reading as true; one may have failed.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuing with a possible air problem risks sudden spring-brake application; stop and get inspected.
distractorExplanations.d: A conflicting warning may mean real air loss; stop safely now rather than driving on.

options.a: Build air to 60 psi, push the knob in, and resume the trip
options.b: Cage the spring brakes and drive to the next shop
options.c: Secure vehicle, diagnose air loss, arrange repair
options.d: Drain the tanks, recharge to cut-out, and continue

distractorExplanations.a: Resetting the springs without finding the air loss lets it happen again at speed.
distractorExplanations.b: Caging removes the emergency/parking brakes; the vehicle should be repaired or towed.
distractorExplanations.d: Draining and recharging does not fix the leak that caused the emergency application.

cdl-air-brakes-readiness-check-failures-.explanation: Fix the air problem first. Do not keep driving normally after an emergency spring application.
